job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Priya Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Priya, and thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We live above our family's corner shop in Oakham, my parents, my grandmother and me, and my day starts at six when the newspapers arrive. I help open the shop, stack shelves and do the till until about ten. Then I go upstairs, apply for accounting jobs, and write the shop's weekly sales in a ledger, which my father calls my real work. In the evening I cook with my grandmother and we go to our congregation's meeting on Thursdays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and why did you choose it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did a bachelor of commerce in accounting at Oakham College and passed with an average mark. My parents wanted me to have a profession so I'd never have to stand in a shop all day, which is ironic now. My final project was a cost analysis of our own shop, and I found we lose money on fresh milk, so we changed the supplier. I had no internship because the shop needed me every holiday. I've sent about forty applications in eight months, had two interviews and no offer. The loan is heavy, my savings are about two weeks of costs, and the shop gives my parents only a thin living, so there's no money for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what I'd expect. People get carried away by new machines, and then life goes on much as before. I'd tell my father that the shop doesn't need to change, and he'd be relieved. I wouldn't post anything online, that's not my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it means my problem stays my problem. The shortage of jobs in Oakham stays, the big firms still take people from the famous universities, and the loan stays. I'd rather have a world where honest work gets rewarded, and this doesn't seem to be one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with applications, around eight a week, to the small accounting firms and the credit union in town, and I'd ask my father's friend Mr Kaplan, who runs a tax office, whether I could shadow him for free to learn. I'd keep doing the shop's books and the ledger, and offer to do the books for other shops on our street. And I'd pay the loan whatever I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, but not afraid. My grandmother says a person who works is never poor, so I keep working. Still, I feel ashamed when neighbours ask why the accountant is stacking tins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think about people who say AI will change everything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A tax office, a small firm that does payroll, even a clerk's job at the town hall. I know how a shop's money works, I've done it for years, and I'd rather do that for a living than sit in a big city office with strangers. The apprenticeship idea suits me, learning beside someone and being paid a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the shop's income dropped further?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut our own small things, like the shop's evening opening hours, and I'd stop my phone contract. My mother already skips her bus pass. I'd never ask the church for money, though, even if the neighbours would help. It's a matter of pride, and I know that's not always sensible.

say: I'd say people **get carried away** by new machines, and life goes on much as before.
I wouldn't post anything online, which isn't my way.
think: My problem stays my problem: few jobs in Oakham and big firms taking **famous university** graduates.
I'd like a world where honest work gets rewarded.
do: Send about eight applications a week to small accounting firms and the **credit union**.
Ask Mr Kaplan, who runs a tax office, to let me shadow him for free.
Offer to keep the books for other **shops on our street**.
feel: Tired but not afraid, and **ashamed** when neighbours ask why the accountant stacks tins.

fieldNote: Values **honest work** and apprenticeship over handouts, in line with her family and faith.

steps.text: Send eight applications a week to small firms and the credit union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be careful and not rush to throw people out of work. I'd say firms owe their staff a chance to learn the new ways. At the congregation, I'd ask people to look out for those who lose their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. Booking, checking and planning are what accounting juniors do, and my degree trained me for exactly that. I'm already slow with new technology, and I've never used the AI tools. I'd be a beginner at the same time as everyone is expected to be an expert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to learn something, even if reluctantly. I'd ask Mr Kaplan to show me the software his office uses, because learning beside a person I trust is easier than alone on a screen. I'd also look at trades-like office work that needs a person in the room, like paying wages and visiting customers. And I'd keep helping in the shop, which would stay the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. It feels like being asked to jump a stream while carrying a heavy basket. I'd pray about it and then get on with the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of those tasks happen in your family's shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ordering, the sales records and the supplier invoices. A cheaper system could do all of that, and some of the big chains already do. But our family shop is about people who come in for a chat and a loaf. That part, no machine can do, and it keeps us going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your parents feel about you changing course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd say stay close to home and find something steady. My father would say it's a pity to have wasted three years, but my mother would say I should do whatever pays. They'd never push me to leave Oakham, because they'd miss me and need me in the shop.

I'd ask my congregation to look out for those who lose jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that this is too fast for ordinary people, and our leaders must slow it down or protect people. I'd ask the congregation to pray, and I'd write to our town councillor. Mostly I'd say, look after one another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel the ground drop out. Two years isn't enough time for me to learn a whole new field, and my degree would be wasted. I don't use the tools, and I'm not quick at new things. I'd feel like I'm already behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put everything into the shop and the family. I'd work longer hours there, and I'd stop applying for accounting jobs that won't exist. I'd cut every cost I could, and I'd ask the loan office about deferral. I'd also look at care or education work, because those need people, and our community needs carers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but I try to keep my face calm because of my parents. At night I'd feel my heart beating in my ears. I'd light a candle for my grandmother and say very little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents and grandmother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grandmother first, since she's seen worse years. She'd say we've survived before. My parents I'd tell more carefully, that I'd be staying in the shop for a while and that I'm sorry about the degree. They'd say never be sorry for learning, but I'd still feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stay the same for the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop's door would still open at six and people would still come for bread. The robots take three more years to do hands-on work, so shelf stacking and the till would be mine for a while. The accounts would be easy for a machine, but the customers don't want a machine, they want us.

I'd write to the town councillor.

feel: **Frightened**, with a calm face for my parents and a racing heart at night.
S2.quote: Two years isn't enough time for me to learn a whole new field, and my degree would be wasted.
fieldNote: Falls back on **family and faith**, with the shop as shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for us to prepare if we act together. I'd ask the congregation to organise skills classes, and I'd say families should look after the young. I'd say it with some hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I could manage if I get a first job soon. I could learn by doing, beside someone, over a couple of years, and I'd have a few working years before the thinking jobs go. But I'd have to be in a place where the work needs trust, like a small practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any role in a local firm, even an assistant, and learn from a person there. I'd save fifty pounds a month, and I'd start using the AI tools in small steps, with Mr Kaplan beside me. I'd keep the shop shifts. And I'd tell my grandmother to practise her card payments, because she refuses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with some fear. It's better to have time and honest warning, like a letter before a visit. I'd feel I could prepare the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years allow that two wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learning slowly, beside a person I trust. In two years, I'd be rushing and fearful. In five, I could do one small thing each month, like using the tool to draft a letter, and then check it. I'd learn it the way I learned the till.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your view of the tools change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably still not like the tools, but I'd understand them. I'd say they're like the new scanners we got in the shop: cold, quick and useful. I don't need to love them, but I need to use them. That would be a change for me.

I'd say it with some hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have plenty of time if we're sensible, and that families and communities should teach each other. I'd say it in the congregation and I'd offer to help older people with their forms. I'd feel quite calm saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I can still build a decent life. By thirty-three I'd like to be a qualified accountant, married, and perhaps running a small practice with my own name on the door. It takes patience, but ten years is enough for patience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd find a job, pay my parents back for what they spent on me, and start the professional exams with an employer's help. I'd save a hundred a month and pay the loan down. I'd learn the tools when my employer needs them, not before. And I'd keep the shop's books forever, for my father.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quiet and content, mostly. I'd have my worries, but I wouldn't feel on a cliff edge. I'd feel there is a path that fits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you hope for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A job that matches my degree, a small flat near the shop, my grandmother seeing me settle, and a family some day. And the shop still open. That's a good life, a modest one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your cousins who are still at school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to study something that fits their hands and heart, and to learn a trade or a profession where people trust them. I'd say don't take loans lightly, as I did. And I'd tell them to use the computers, because I was slow, and I regret it.

I'd offer to help older people with their forms.
think: I can still build a **decent life**: a qualified accountant by thirty-three with my name on the door.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because I'm slow with new things and there'd be no time to learn. What would help is a deferral on the loan, an apprenticeship where I learn beside someone, and neighbours looking after one another. The honest warning would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't asking for charity. We'd like honest work and a fair chance to learn. If somebody could give a young person like me a place and some patience, I'd work harder than anyone.

headlineQuote: If somebody could give a young person like me a place and some patience, I'd work harder than anyone.
portrait: Priya (23) lives above her family's corner shop in **Oakham** with her parents and grandmother.
She holds a pass in commerce and accounting, owes a heavy loan and has about two weeks of savings.
She is traditional and faith-minded, values **honest work**, and has never used AI tools.
She relies on **family, her congregation** and learning beside a trusted person rather than alone.
She grows calmer only when there are years to learn slowly and a first job arrives.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most because she is slow with new things and would have no time to learn.
whatWouldHelp: A **loan deferral**, an apprenticeship beside a trusted person and honest warning.
